[Intervention Review]
Interventions for BK virus infection in kidney transplant recipients
Zainab Wajih1, Krishna M Karpe2, Giles D Walters2
1Renal and General Medicine, Bathurst Hospital (WNSWLHD), Bathurst, NSW, Australia. 2Department of Renal Medicine, The Canberra
Hospital, Canberra, Australia
Contact: Zainab Wajih, zainab_wajih@hotmail.com.
Editorial group: Cochrane Kidney and Transplant Group.
Publication status and date: New, published in Issue 10, 2024.
Citation: Wajih Z, Karpe KM, Walters GD. Interventions for BK virus infection in kidney transplant recipients. Cochrane Database of
Systematic Reviews 2024, Issue 10. Art. No.: CD013344. DOI: 10.1002/14651858.CD013344.pub2.
Copyright © 2024 The Cochrane Collaboration. Published by John Wiley & Sons, Ltd.
A B S T R A C T
Background
BK virus-associated nephropathy (BKVAN), caused by infection with or reactivation of BK virus, remains a challenge in kidney
transplantation. Screening is recommended for all kidney transplant recipients. For those with clinically significant infection, reduction of
immunosuppression is the cornerstone of management. There is no specific antiviral or immunomodulatory therapy suficiently efective
for routine use.
Objectives
This review aimed to examine the benefits and harms of interventions for BK virus infection in kidney transplant recipients.
Search methods
We searched the Cochrane Kidney and Transplant Register of Studies up to 5 September 2024 through contact with the Information
Specialist using search terms relevant to this review. Studies in the Register are identified through searches of CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and
EMBASE, conference proceedings, the International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP) Search Portal and ClinicalTrials.gov.
Selection criteria
All randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and cohort studies investigating any intervention for the treatment or prevention of BKVAN for
kidney transplant recipients.
Data collection and analysis
Two authors independently assessed the study quality and extracted data. Summary estimates of efect were obtained using a random-
efects model, and results were expressed as risk ratios (RR) and their 95% confidence intervals (CI) for dichotomous outcomes and mean
diference (MD) and 95% CI for continuous outcomes. Confidence in the evidence was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations
Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach.
Main results
Twelve RCTs (2669 randomised participants) were included. Six studies were undertaken in single centres, and six were multicentre studies;
two of these were international studies. The ages of those participating ranged from 44 to 57 years. The length of follow-up ranged from
three months to five years. All studies included people with a kidney transplant, and three studies included people with signs of BK
viraemia. Studies were heterogeneous in terms of the type of interventions and outcomes assessed. The overall risk of bias was low or
unclear.

Intensive screening for the early detection of BK viraemia or BK viruria prevents graf loss (1 study, 908 participants: RR 0.00, 95% CI 0.00 to
0.05) and decreases the presence of decoy cells and viraemia at 12 months (1 study, 908 participants: RR 0.06, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.11) compared
to routine care (high certainty evidence). No other outcomes were reported.
Compared to placebo, fluoroquinolones may slightly reduce the risk of graf loss (3 studies, 393 participants: RR 0.37, CI 0.09 to 1.57; I2 =
0%; low certainty evidence), probably makes little or no diference to donor-specific antibodies (DSA), may make little or no diference to
BK viraemia and death, had uncertain efects on BKVAN and malignancy, but may increase the risk of tendonitis (2 studies, 193 participants:
RR 5.66, CI 1.02 to 31.32; I2 = 0%; low certainty evidence).
Compared to tacrolimus (TAC), cyclosporin (CSA) probably makes little or no diference to graf loss and death, may make little or no
diference to BKVAN and malignancy, but probably decreases BK viraemia (2 studies, 263 participants: RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.26 to 1.41; I2 =
38%) and probably reduces the risk of new-onset diabetes afer transplantation (1 study, 200 participants: RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.12 to 1.35)
(both moderate certainty evidence).
Compared to azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) probably makes little or no diference to graf loss and BK viraemia but probably
reduces the risk of death (1 study, 133 participants: RR 0.43, 95% CI 0.16 to 1.16) and malignancy (1 study, 199 participants: RR 0.43, 95%
CI 0.16 to 1.16) (both moderate certainty evidence).
Compared to mycophenolate sodium (MPS), CSA has uncertain efects on graf loss and death, may make little or no diference to BK
viraemia, but may reduce BKVAN (1 study, 224 participants: RR 0.06, 95% CI 0.00 to 1.20; low certainty evidence).
Compared to immunosuppression dose reduction, MMF or TAC conversion to everolimus or sirolimus may make little or no diference to
graf loss, BK viraemia or BKVAN (low certainty evidence). TAC conversion to sirolimus probably results in more people having a reduced BK
viral load (< 600 copies/mL) than immunosuppression reduction (1 study, 30 participants: RR 1.31, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.89; moderate certainty
evidence).
Compared to MPS, everolimus had uncertain efects on graf loss and BK viraemia, may reduce BKVAN (1 study, 135 participants: 0.06, 95%
CI 0.00 to 1.11) and may increase the risk of death (1 study, 135 participants: RR 3.71, 95% CI 0.20 to 67.35) (both low certainty evidence).
Compared to CSA, everolimus may make little or no diference to BK viraemia, has uncertain efects on graf loss and BKVAN, but may
increase the risk of death (1 study, 185 participants: RR 3.71, 95% CI 0.42 to 32.55; low certainty evidence).
Compared to immunosuppression reduction, the leflunomide derivative FK778 may make little or no diference to graf loss, probably
results in a greater reduction in plasma BK viral load (1 study, 44 participants: -0.60 copies/µL, 95% CI -1.22 to 0.02; moderate certainty
evidence), but had uncertain efects on BKVAN and malignancy. Aggravated hypertension may be increased with KF778 (1 study, 46
participants: RR 8.23, 95% CI 0.50 to 135.40; low certainty evidence). There were no deaths in either group.
Authors' conclusions
Intense monitoring early afer transplantation for BK viruria and BK viraemia is efective in improving BK virus infection outcomes as it
helps with early detection of the infection and allows for a timely reduction in immunosuppression reduction. There is insuficient evidence
to support any other intervention for BK virus infection in kidney transplant recipients.
P L A I N   L A N G U A G E   S U M M A R Y
What interventions help to prevent or treat BK virus infection in kidney transplant recipients?
Key messages
• People who have received a transplanted kidney because of kidney failure (a condition where the kidneys no longer function well
enough to keep a person alive) are at risk of infection. This is because they have to take strong medications to dampen down the body's
immune system (immunosuppressants) to prevent their body from fighting (rejecting) this new kidney. This puts them at risk of developing
infection, which may afect the way the new kidney functions. A virus (BK virus) with symptoms similar to the common cold is ofen picked
up early in life and then stays dormant in the body. When the body's immune system is suppressed, this virus can once again become active.
• Intensive screening for BK virus infection in the blood or urine and then the early reduction in the dose of immunosuppressants prevented
the loss of the transplanted kidney and reduced the amount of BK virus in the blood at 1 year. Our confidence in the efect of other
interventions is low, with most making little or no diference to the loss of the transplanted kidney, the amount of BK virus in the blood,
and new kidney disease associated with BK virus. Side efects were poorly reported.
What is BK virus?
BK virus has symptoms like the common cold and most people come in contact with it during childhood. Once a person gets BK virus
infection, the virus will stay in the body for the rest of their life and usually stays dormant (like being asleep). It does not normally cause a
problem; however, for people whose immune system (the body's mechanism for fighting anything foreign) does not work well, the virus

can wake up. People who have received a kidney transplant because of kidney failure (a condition where the kidneys no longer function
well enough to keep a person alive) have to take strong medicines to prevent their body from trying to fight (or reject) this new kidney.
These medicines dampen down the immune system (immunosuppressants), and the BK virus may once again become active and may
afect the new kidney.
What did we want to find out?
We wanted to find out if interventions aimed at preventing BK virus infection or interventions aimed at treating BK virus infections help
prevent the loss of the transplanted kidney, reduce the amount of BK virus in the blood (viraemia), and prevent kidney disease associated
with the BK virus. We also wanted to find out if these interventions were associated with any unwanted efects.
What did we do?
We searched for all studies that looked at the benefits and harms of interventions aimed at either preventing or treating BK virus infection.
We compared and summarised the results of the studies and rated our confidence in the information based on factors such as study
methods and sizes.
What did we find?
We found 12 studies involving 2669 people with a kidney transplant. Six studies were undertaken in single centres, and six were multicentre
studies; 2 of these were international studies. The ages of those participating ranged from 44 to 57 years. The length of follow-up ranged
from 3 months to 5 years. All studies included people with a kidney transplant, and 3 studies included people with signs of BK viraemia.
Interventions included very close monitoring (intensive screening) for BK virus in the blood and urine followed by early changes to the
immunosuppressants if detected, changing the dose or types of immunosuppressants used once the BK virus was detected, and antibiotics
(fluoroquinolones) for preventing and treating BK viraemia.
Intensive screening for BK virus infection and then the early reduction in the dose of immunosuppressants prevented the loss of the
transplanted kidney and reduced the amount of BK virus in the blood at 1 year. The efect of other interventions varied, with most making
little or no diference to the loss of the transplanted kidney, BK viraemia and kidney disease associated with the BK virus. Side efects were
poorly reported.
What are the limitations of the evidence?
We are confident that intensive screening for BK virus prevents the loss of the transplanted kidney and helps decrease the amount of BK
virus in the blood. Our confidence in the results of the other interventions is low to very low because of the small number of studies (per
comparison) and the small size of the studies. Not all the studies provided data for the outcomes we were interested in or were reported
in a way that we could not analyse.
How up-to-date is the evidence?
The evidence is current to 5 September 2024.

B A C K G R O U N D
Description of the condition
Kidney transplantation continues to be the treatment of choice
for patients with kidney failure due to the survival benefit in
comparison with patients remaining on dialysis (Wolfe 1999).
The potent immunosuppression regimens that are currently used
have been relatively successful in reducing acute rejection and
preserving the kidney transplant. However, over-suppression of the
immune system has been associated with the emergence of BK
virus infection (Brennan 2005; Hirsch 2005; Schold 2009).
BK virus is a small DNA virus that establishes lifelong infection in
the renal tubular and uroepithelial cells of most of the world's
population. For the majority, infection is quiescent and benign.
BK virus previously belonged to the Polyomavirus genus of
the Papovaviridae family, which consisted of papillomavirus and
polyomavirus. In 1999, the International Committee on Taxonomy
of Virus classified it into the Polyomaviridae family (DeCaprio 2013).
It is believed that primary BK virus infection occurs in the early
decade of life. The overall immunoglobulin G (IgG) seroprevalence
of BKV is approximately 82% (Egli 2009). Direct person-to-person
contact or exposure to contaminated surfaces, foods and water has
been considered the likely method of transmission (Hirsch 2014).
The virus persists within the kidney tissue (Heritage 1981) and
mostly does not cause any symptoms until it is reactivated (Hirsch
2002; Hirsch 2014). Interestingly, the data supports the donor origin
of the infection in kidney transplant recipients (Bohl 2005).
Among kidney transplant recipients, BK virus reactivation is
common. Reactivation is frequently subclinical, although it may
manifest with acute kidney injury (AKI), and is a risk factor
for premature allograf loss. BK virus-associated nephropathy
(BKVAN) is an emerging cause of kidney transplant failure
afecting 1% to 10% of patients (Hirsch 2002). Thus, screening
for reactivation is recommended for all kidney transplant
recipients afer transplantation. There is no specific antiviral or
immunomodulatory therapy suficiently efective for routine use.
For those with clinically significant reactivation, reduction of
immunosuppression is the cornerstone of management.
In the modern immunosuppression era, 95% of cases of BKVAN are
caused by BK virus and 5% by human polyomavirus 2 (formerly JC
virus or John Cunningham virus) (Gonzalez 2015; Sawinski 2015b;
Schwarz 2012). Without intervention, more than 90% of kidney
transplant patients with BKVAN show a decline in allograf function,
which is followed by graf loss in at least 50% of cases (Hirsch 2014).
Risk factors associated with BK virus infection include human
leucocyte antigen (HLA) mismatch, deceased donor, degree of
ischaemia-reperfusion, female donor and male recipients, older
age of recipients, ureteral stent insertion, acute rejection episodes,
and immunosuppressive therapy (rabbit anti-thymocyte globulin
(ATG) as induction with tacrolimus (TAC), mycophenolate mofetil
(MMF), or both as maintenance immunosuppression) (Borni-Duval
2013; Brennan 2005; Bressollette-Bodin 2005; Dharnidharka 2009;
Gonzalez 2015; Hirsch 2005; Hirsch 2014; Pham 2014; Prince 2009;
Schold 2009; Siparsky 2011). Additionally, a cohort study found
that donor BK virus-neutralising serostatus is a strong predictor
of the risk of post-transplant BK viraemia regardless of recipient-
neutralising serostatus (Abend 2017). The absence of the HLA C7
allele in either the donor or recipient has also been associated
with an increased risk of sustained BK viraemia (Bohl 2005). In
contrast, African-American ethnicity has been associated with a
lower prevalence of BK virus infection (Sood 2012).
Renal biopsy with characteristic viral cytopathic changes in tubular
epithelial cells and Simian Virus 40 immunohistochemistry is
considered the gold standard for BKVAN diagnosis (Nickeleit 2018).
Moreover, it provides the degree of chronic damage, which can
predict graf prognosis (Drachenberg 2004).
BK virus detection by real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR)
of plasma with a threshold of 4.1 log 10 copies/mL has 100%
sensitivity, ~90% specificity, 50% positive-predictive value and
negative predictive value of 100% in BKVAN diagnosis (Bechert
2010; Pollara 2011; Viscount 2007). The current standard of care
recommends all kidney transplant recipients should be screened
for BKPyV-DNAemia monthly until month nine, and then every
three months until two years post-transplant. Extended screening
afer two years may be considered in paediatric transplant
recipients (Hirsh 2019). However, various factors contributing to
the inter-assay variability in measuring BK viral loads are the
diferences in sample type (urine versus plasma versus whole
blood), DNA extraction and purification methods, diferences in
primer and probe sequences, diferences in viral strains and
sequences, diferent DNA preparation and PCR amplification
conditions (Bechert 2010; Hofman 2008; Randhawa 2011).
Therefore, it is recommended to monitor from the same laboratory.
On the other hand, BK virus detection by PCR of urine with
a threshold of 2.5 x 10-7 copies/mL has 100% sensitivity, 92%
specificity, 31% positive predictive value, and 100% negative
predictive value. Furthermore, the presence of decoy cells in urine
samples has 25% sensitivity and 84% specificity (Bechert 2010;
Viscount 2007). The caveat for urine examination is that there is
no increased risk of BKVAN in a patient with elevated BK viral load
in the urine without the presence of BK viraemia (Brennan 2005;
Hirsch 2014).
Management of BK virus infection has been complicated. Most
of the literature reiterates the importance of immunosuppression
reduction (Brennan 2005; Hardinger 2010; Schaub 2010). However,
this will expose the kidney transplant recipients to an increased
risk of acute rejection, which will subsequently reduce the overall
graf and patient survival. Additionally, persistent BK viraemia
has been strongly associated with de novo class 2 donor-specific
antibody (DSA) production (Sawinski 2015a). Retransplantation
following allograf loss due to BKVAN has been reviewed as a
possible treatment option. The data from the Organ Procurement
and Transplantation Network described excellent short-term graf
and patient survival of 94% and 98%, respectively (Dharnidharka
2010). Transplant nephrectomy has not been shown to ofer any
protection against recurrent BK virus replication. However, the
clearance of BK viraemia before re-transplantation should be
achieved before surgery (Dharnidharka 2010; Trofe-Clark 2016).
A systematic review published in 2010 found a death-censored
graf loss rate of 8/100 patient-years for immune suppression alone
and 8/100 and 13/100 patient-years for the addition of cidofovir or
leflunomide, respectively (Johnston 2010).

Description of the intervention
The mainstay of therapy for BKV infection is to improve BK
virus-specific immunity by reducing the intensity of maintenance
immunosuppression or administering medication with an antiviral
efect. The usual strategies in treating BKVAN are reducing the
dose of calcineurin inhibitors ((CNI), TAC, cyclosporin (CSA)) or
mycophenolate (MMF; sodium: MPS), cessation of azathioprine
(AZA) or MMF, concomitant reduction of both CNI and anti-
metabolite, switching of CNI to mammalian target of rapamycin
(mTOR) inhibitor, and switching of TAC to CSA. Drugs with
anti-polyoma efects, such as cidofovir, leflunomide, leflunomide
derivative FK778, and fluoroquinolones, have also been used to
enhance viral clearance, suppression or both. Some studies have
also incorporated intravenous (IV) IgG into the regimen.
How the intervention might work
As BK virus reactivation typically occurs within the first two
years post-transplantation, during which the patient receives
a significantly higher dose of immunosuppression to prevent
rejection, reduction of immunosuppression can theoretically
improve viral clearance. Reduction of immunosuppression
can include reducing the dose or switching to less potent
immunosuppressive agents.
Leflunomide, a pyrimidine synthesis inhibitor, has been developed
as a treatment for rheumatoid arthritis. Its metabolite has been
shown to have antiviral properties against DNA viruses, such as
cytomegalovirus (CMV) (Waldman 1999).
The leflunomide derivative FK778 has been shown to have
antiviral activity against polyomavirus. Additionally, it reversibly
binds to dihydro-orotate-dehydrogenase, resulting in pyrimidine
biosynthesis inhibition, which was shown to prevent acute allograf
rejection in experimental transplantation models in non-humans
(Schorlemmer 2001).
Fluoroquinolones have been proposed as a potential therapy for BK
virus infection due to in vitro data. It has activity against large T-
antigen BK virus helicase (Sharma 2011).
Cidofovir, a nucleoside analogue, decreases CMV replication by
inhibiting viral DNA polymerase. It also has in vitro activity against
BK virus, but its mechanism of action appears to be inhibition of
intracellular BK virus genome replication (Bernhof 2008).
Commercially available preparation of IV immunoglobulin (IVIG)
contains high titres of neutralising antibodies against BK virus.
These antibodies have direct neutralising activity against BK virus
(Randhawa 2006).
Why it is important to do this review
The management of BK virus infection remains a challenge.
Interventions are frequently multi-modal (e.g. reduction of first-line
immunosuppression, conversion to another immunosuppressive
agent, additional therapies), making it dificult to distinguish the
individual efect of each intervention on the outcome. Antivirals
have been recommended in the literature; however, there is
no definitive evidence of benefit with these agents. Most of
the literature reiterates the importance of immunosuppression
reduction. However, this may expose kidney transplant recipients
to an increased risk of acute rejection, which may subsequently
reduce the overall graf and patient survival.
O B J E C T I V E S
We aimed to examine the benefits and harms of interventions for
BK virus infection in kidney transplant recipients.
M E T H O D S
Criteria for considering studies for this review
Types of studies
All randomised controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-RCTs (RCTs in which
treatment allocation was obtained by alternation, use of alternate
medical records, date of birth or other predictable methods) and
cohort studies were included.
Types of participants
Inclusion criteria
We included patients who received a primary or repeat kidney
transplant from a deceased or living donor. Patients were included
if there was documented BK viruria based on positive BK PCR from a
urine sample, BK viraemia or biopsy-proven BKVAN and/or received
a specific intervention (immunosuppression reduction, antiviral,
antibiotic, leflunomide, mTOR inhibitor or combination therapy) to
reduce BK viraemia or prevent BKVAN.
Exclusion criteria
Recipients of non-kidney or dual organ transplants were excluded.
Case reports were not included.
Types of interventions
We included studies addressing interventions to treat BK virus
infection, including BK viraemia and BK viruria, as well as biopsy-
proven BKVAN. Comparisons included:
1. Intensive screening versus routine care
2. Fluoroquinolones versus placebo
3. CSA versus TAC
4. MMF versus AZA
5. CSA versus MPS
6. MMF conversion to everolimus versus MMF dose reduction
7. Conversion to TAC plus everolimus versus TAC plus MMF
8. TAC conversion to sirolimus versus immunosuppression
reduction
9. Everolimus versus MPS
10.Everolimus versus CSA
11.Leflunomide derivative FK778 versus standard care (reduced
immunosuppression).
Types of outcome measures
The outcomes selected include the relevant SONG core outcome
sets as specified by the Standardised Outcomes in Nephrology
initiative (SONG 2017).
Primary outcomes
Graf health or survival

Search methods for identification of studies
Electronic searches
We searched the Cochrane Kidney and Transplant Register of
Studies up to 5 September 2024 through contact with the
Information Specialist using search terms relevant to this review.
The Register contains studies identified from the following sources.
1. Monthly searches of the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled
Trials (CENTRAL)
2. Weekly searches of MEDLINE OVID SP
3. Hand searching of kidney-related journals and the proceedings
of major kidney conferences
4. Searching the current year of EMBASE OVID SP
5. Weekly current awareness alerts for selected kidney and
transplant journals
6. Searches of the International Clinical Trials Registry Platform
(ICTRP) Search Portal and ClinicalTrials.gov.
Studies contained in the Register are identified through searches of
CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE based on the scope of Cochrane
Kidney and Transplant. Details of search strategies, as well as
a list of hand-searched journals, conference proceedings and
current awareness alerts, are available on the Cochrane Kidney and
Transplant website.
See Appendix 1 for search terms used in strategies for this review.
Searching other resources
1. Reference lists of review articles, relevant studies and clinical
practice guidelines.
2. Contact experts and organisations in the field seeking
information about unpublished or incomplete studies.
3. Grey literature sources (e.g. abstracts, dissertations and theses),
in addition to those already included in the Cochrane Kidney and
Transplant Register of Studies, were not searched.
Data collection and analysis
Selection of studies
The search strategy described was used to obtain titles and
abstracts of studies that may be relevant to the review. The titles
and abstracts were screened independently by two authors, who
discarded studies that did not meet inclusion criteria, although
studies and reviews that might include relevant data or information
on studies were retained initially. Two authors independently
assessed abstracts and, if necessary, the full text of these studies to
determine which studies satisfied the inclusion criteria.
Data extraction and management
Data extraction was carried out by the same authors independently
using standard data extraction forms. Where more than one
publication of one study exists, reports were grouped together,
and the publication with the most complete data was used in the
analyses. Where relevant outcomes were only published in earlier
versions, these data were used.
Assessment of risk of bias in included studies
For RCTs, the following items were independently assessed by
two authors using the risk of bias assessment tool (Higgins 2022)
(Appendix 2).
•
Was there adequate sequence generation (selection bias)?
•
Was allocation adequately concealed (selection bias)?
•
Was knowledge of the allocated interventions adequately
prevented during the study?
◦ Participants and personnel (performance bias)
◦ Outcome assessors (detection bias)
•
Was incomplete outcome data adequately addressed (attrition
bias)?
•
Are reports of the study free of suggestion of selective outcome
reporting (reporting bias)?
•
Was the study free of other problems that could put it at risk of
bias?
For 
non-randomised 
studies,

use
the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) (www.ohri.ca/programs/
clinical_epidemiology/nosgen.pdf) to assess quality (Appendix 3;
Appendix 4).
•
Selection: representativeness of the exposed cohort, selection
of the non-exposed cohort, ascertainment of exposure,
demonstration that outcome of interest was not present at the
start of the study
•
Potential confounding factors are underlying kidney pathology,
post-transplant diabetes mellitus, live versus cadaveric
donation, number of HLA mismatches, and ABO-compatibility
•
Comparability: comparability of cohorts on the basis of the
design or analysis
•
Outcome: assessment of outcome, adequacy of follow-up and
duration of follow-up.
No cohort studies were included.
Measures of treatment efect
For dichotomous outcomes such as viral clearance, acute rejection,
graf survival, patient survival, and therapy-related adverse events,
results are expressed as risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence
intervals (CI). Where continuous outcomes were reported (e.g. SCr,
eGFR), the mean diference (MD) was used.

Unit of analysis issues
If multiple groups are investigated in one study, we used each group
only once in the review. Data were compared on similar scales.
For RCTs with repeated measurements, we considered the longest
follow-up for the analysis
Dealing with missing data
Evaluation of important numerical data such as screened,
randomised patients, as well as intention-to-treat, as-treated and
per-protocol population, was carefully performed. Attrition rates,
for example, drop-outs, losses to follow-up and withdrawals were
investigated. Issues of missing data and imputation methods
(e.g. last-observation-carried-forward) were critically appraised
(Higgins 2022).
Assessment of heterogeneity
We first assessed the heterogeneity by visual inspection of the
forest plot. We then quantified statistical heterogeneity using the
I2 statistic, which describes the percentage of total variation across
studies that is due to heterogeneity rather than sampling error
(Higgins 2003). A guide to the interpretation of I2 values is as follows.
•
0% to 40%: might not be important
•
30% to 60%: may represent moderate heterogeneity
•
50% to 90%: may represent substantial heterogeneity
•
75% to 100%: considerable heterogeneity.
The importance of the observed value of I2 depends on the
magnitude and direction of treatment efects and the strength of
evidence for heterogeneity (e.g. P value from the Chi2 test, or a CI
for I2) (Higgins 2022).
Studies were assessed based on their patient populations,
treatments, and outcomes to decide whether meta-analysis
is appropriate. Non-randomised studies were to be assessed
separately but similarly to give maximum insight into available
data. By default, standard outcomes are represented in forest plots
with or without totals for overall efect.
Assessment of reporting biases
We planned to assess the possibility of publication bias for every
outcome studied, but there were too few studies to allow a
meaningful evaluation.
Data synthesis
Data were pooled using the random-efects model.
Subgroup analysis and investigation of heterogeneity
Because insuficient studies compared the same pair of
interventions, we were unable to explore whether there were
diferences in the following study-level characteristics; participants
(age, gender, renal pathology and kidney function at presentation),
treatments and study quality variability. The risk diference with
95% CI was to be calculated for each adverse efect, either
compared to no treatment or another agent; there were insuficient
studies to do this.
Sensitivity analysis
We planned to perform sensitivity analyses; however, there were
insuficient observations to do this.
Summary of findings and assessment of the certainty of the
evidence
We present the main results of the review in summary of findings
(SOF) tables. These tables present key information concerning
the quality of the evidence, the magnitude of the efects of the
interventions examined, and the sum of the available data for
the main outcomes (Schünemann 2022a). The SOF tables also
include an overall grading of the evidence related to each of the
main outcomes using the Grades of Recommendation, Assessment,
Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach (GRADE 2008;
GRADE 2011). The GRADE approach defines the quality of a body
of evidence as the extent to which one can be confident that
an estimate of efect or association is close to the true quantity
of specific interest. The quality of a body of evidence involves
consideration of the within-trial risk of bias (methodological
quality), directness of evidence, heterogeneity, the precision of
efect estimates and risk of publication bias (Schünemann 2022b).
We present the following outcomes in the SOF tables.
•
Graf survival (e.g. graf loss, rejection)
•
Change in BK viral load (viraemia, viruria or similar)
•
BKVAN
•
Development of de-novo DSA
•
Death
•
Therapy-related adverse events
•
Malignancy

Description of studies
The following section contains broad descriptions of the studies

Results of the search
Afer searching the Specialised Register, a total of 178 records
were identified. Afer screening titles and abstracts and then full-
text review, 12 RCTs (67 reports) were included, and 11 studies
(93 reports) were excluded. Five ongoing studies were identified
(5 reports) and six studies (13 reports) were identified prior to
publication. These 11 studies will be assessed in a future update of
this review (Figure 1). No cohort studies were identified.

Included studies
Twelve studies (2669 randomised participants) were included.
Study characteristics
Six studies were single-centre studies (Brennan 2005; Galen 2014;
Patel 2019; Renner 2013; Wali 2008; Wojciechowski 2017) and six
were multicentre (DIRECT TX 2005; Guasch 2010; Humar 2013; Lee
2014; MECANO 2009; Mohan 2016). Studies were undertaken in
Canada (Humar 2013), Germany (Renner 2013), the Netherlands
(MECANO 2009), and the USA (Brennan 2005; Galen 2014; Lee 2014;
Mohan 2016; Patel 2019; Wali 2008; Wojciechowski 2017), and two
studies were international studies (DIRECT TX 2005; Guasch 2010).
The mean age range was 44 to 57 years. All studies enrolled kidney
transplant recipients, and three studies also included patients with
BKVAN (Guasch 2010) or BK viraemia (Lee 2014; Wojciechowski
2017).

Random sequence generation
Randomisation methods were adequately reported in four studies
(DIRECT TX 2005; Guasch 2010; Humar 2013; Patel 2019) and unclear
in eight studies (Brennan 2005; Galen 2014; Lee 2014; MECANO
2009; Mohan 2016; Renner 2013; Wali 2008 Wojciechowski 2017).
Allocation concealment
Allocation concealment was judged to be low in two studies
(DIRECT TX 2005; Humar 2013) and unclear in 10 studies (Brennan
2005; Galen 2014; Guasch 2010; Lee 2014; MECANO 2009; Mohan
2016; Patel 2019; Renner 2013; Wali 2008; Wojciechowski 2017).
Blinding
Performance bias (participants and study personnel)
Performance bias was judged to be low in three studies (Humar
2013; Lee 2014; Patel 2019), high in seven studies (Brennan 2005;
DIRECT TX 2005; Guasch 2010; Galen 2014; MECANO 2009; Mohan
2016; Wojciechowski 2017), and unclear in two studies (Renner
2013; Wali 2008).
Detection bias (outcome assessment)
Detection bias was judged to be low in two studies (Humar 2013;
Lee 2014) and unclear in 10 studies (Brennan 2005; DIRECT TX 2005;
Galen 2014; Guasch 2010; MECANO 2009; Mohan 2016; Patel 2019;
Renner 2013; Wali 2008; Wojciechowski 2017).
Incomplete outcome data
Attrition bias was judged to be low in six studies (Brennan 2005;
DIRECT TX 2005; Guasch 2010; Humar 2013; MECANO 2009; Patel
2019) and unclear in six studies (Galen 2014; Lee 2014; Mohan 2016;
Renner 2013; Wali 2008; Wojciechowski 2017).
Selective reporting
Reporting bias was judged to be low in seven studies (Brennan
2005; DIRECT TX 2005; Guasch 2010; Humar 2013; Lee 2014;
MECANO 2009; Patel 2019) and unclear in five studies (Galen 2014;
Mohan 2016; Renner 2013; Wali 2008; Wojciechowski 2017).
Other potential sources of bias
Other potential sources of bias were judged to be low in six
studies (Brennan 2005; DIRECT TX 2005; Guasch 2010; Humar 2013;
MECANO 2009; Patel 2019) and unclear in four studies (Galen 2014;
Mohan 2016; Renner 2013; Wali 2008).
Two studies were judged to be at high risk of bias: groups appeared
to be slightly unbalanced (sex, prior transplant and median BK viral
load) (Lee 2014), and the TAC trough level was slightly higher in the
MMF dose reduction group (Wojciechowski 2017).

Intensive screening versus routine care
•
Wali 2008 reported no graf loss with intensive screening
compared to routine care (Analysis 1.1, 908 participants: RR 0.00,
95% CI 0.00 to 0.05; high certainty evidence).
•
Wali 2008 reported intensive screening decreases the

evidence).
See Summary of findings 1.
Fluroquinolones versus placebo
Graf health and survival: graf loss, rejection, and kidney function
measures
•
The risk of graf loss may be slightly reduced with
fluoroquinolones (Analysis 2.1 (3 studies, 393 participants): RR
0.37, CI 0.09 to 1.57; I2 = 0%; low certainty evidence).
•
There is probably little or no diference in rejection with
fluoroquinolones compared to placebo (Analysis 2.2 (3 studies,
393 participants): RR 1.13, CI 0.58 to 2.21; I2 = 0%; moderate
certainty evidence).
•
Fluoroquinolone may reduce SCr at six months (2 studies, 193
participants: MD -17.36 µmol/L, 95% CI -59.80 to 25.28; I2 = 50%)
and one year (Humar 2013, 154 participants: MD -7.60 µmol/
L, 95% CI -21.23 to 6.03), but the evidence is very uncertain
(Analysis 2.3).
BK virus infection (viraemia or viruria), BK virus-associated
nephropathy
•
Fluoroquinolones may make little or no diference to BK
viraemia at the end of the study compared to placebo (Analysis
2.4 (3 studies, 383 participants): RR 1.31, 95% CI 0.68 to 2.54; I2

Lee 2014 reported fluoroquinolones may make little or no

participants: RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.34) or six months (40
participants: RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.41) (Analysis 2.5).

D I S C U S S I O N
Summary of main results
In this review, we have included 12 RCTs (67 reports) involving 2669
participants reporting on the efects of a range of interventions
for BK virus infection. No cohort studies were included. There
was considerable heterogeneity in the type of interventions,
which included the use of antibiotics, immunomodulators,
immunosuppression reduction, immunosuppression conversion
and intensive screening. There was considerable heterogeneity in
study duration, ranging from six months to four years, and the
length of follow-up, ranging from eight months to five years. The
risk of bias in the included studies was ofen unclear, with some
studies providing insuficient information to assess the risk of bias
accurately. Overall, only one of the 12 studies adequately reported
all domains of risk of bias.
Wali 2008 reported that intensive screening, compared to routine
care, with pre-determined stepwise modification of maintenance
immunosuppression based on cell cytology and viraemia, is
associated with less risk of persistence of decoy cells and viraemia
at 12 months and better graf survival.
Fluoroquinolones may reduce the risk of graf loss and UTIs, may
have little or no efect on BK viraemia at one year, probably make
little or no diference to de novo DSA, have uncertain efects on the
risk of BKVAN, and may increase the risk of tendonitis compared to
placebo (Galen 2014; Humar 2013; Lee 2014; Patel 2019).
CSA probably makes little or no diference to graf loss and death,
probably decreases the risk of BK viraemia, but there may be little
or no diference in the risk of developing BKVAN or malignancies
compared to TAC (Brennan 2005; DIRECT TX 2005; Renner 2013).
Brennan 2005 reported less NODAT with CSA.
Brennan 2005 reported MMF probably makes little or no diference
to the risk of graf loss or the risk of BK viraemia compared to AZA.
The risks of death and malignancy were probably reduced with
MMF.
MECANO 2009 reported BK viruria and BKVAN may be lower with
CSA, may make little or no diference to BK viraemia, and had
uncertain efects on graf loss and death compared to MPS.

Conversion of either MMF or TAC to an mTOR inhibitor may make
little or no diference to graf loss, BK viraemia, BK viruria and
BKVAN (Mohan 2016; Renner 2013; Wojciechowski 2017).
MECANO 2009 reported that compared to MPS, everolimus has
uncertain efects on graf loss and BK viraemia, may reduce the
risk of BKVAN, and may increase the risk of death. Compared to
CSA, everolimus has uncertain efects on graf loss and BKVAN, may
make little or no diference to BK viraemia, but may increase the
risk of death.
Guasch 2010 reported that compared to immunosuppression
reduction, the leflunomide derivative FK778 may make little or no
diference to graf loss but may decrease overall kidney function.
FK778 probably reduces plasma BK viral load, has uncertain efects
on BKVAN, death and malignancy, but may increase aggravated
hypertension.
Overall, the available data in this review provides evidence that
intensive screening for early detection of BK nephropathy allows
for an opportunity to prevent disease progression and graf loss.
This pragmatic approach could be easily integrated into routine
clinical care. The risk of BKVAN amongst the routinely used
immunosuppressants in kidney transplantation is no diferent, and
the use of other agents, such as fluoroquinolones or leflunomide
derivative FK778, does not appear to confer much benefit and may
cause more harm. However, these findings are based on low to
moderate-certainty data, and more high-quality RCTs are required.
Overall completeness and applicability of evidence
The data on interventions for BK nephropathy remains incomplete.
Case reports and series were not included in this review. However,
this review summarises a significant body of research that
represents some moderate to high-quality data which goes some
way to giving guidance on treatment. The studies were of small
size. Moreover, there were no studies evaluating conversion to
belatacept for maintenance immunosuppression as a treatment
strategy.
Quality of the evidence
We assessed the quality of evidence using standard risks of
bias domains specified by the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool and
GRADE methodology. The review is limited by the small number
of available studies answering particular questions and variable
reported outcomes. Overall, the risk of bias was judged to be low
or unclear. Seven studies were open-label and were at high risk of
performance bias, but for study outcomes such as death and graf
loss, they were not downgraded on the GRADE assessment.
Potential biases in the review process
We have attempted to avoid bias in our review process, including
all studies that met the inclusion criteria in this area. They have
been examined with standard processes. We have adhered to our
protocol.
Agreements and disagreements with other studies or
reviews
Comparison with other reviews is dificult as they also analysed
data that was based on non-RCTs.
Song 2016 (1477 participants) was a systematic review and
meta-analysis that investigated fluoroquinolone prophylaxis in
preventing BK virus infection afer kidney transplantation and
suggested that fluoroquinolones are inefective. Their analysis
included RCTs as well as observational studies. Our review also
did not find any benefit from fluoroquinolones for BK viraemia or
BKVAN.
Mallat 2017 (6211 participants) was a systematic review and
meta-analysis that studied CMV and BKPyV infections in kidney
transplant recipients receiving an mTOR inhibitor-based regimen
versus a CNI-based regimen and concluded that the available
evidence neither confirmed nor ruled out a reduction of BK virus
infection in the mTOR inhibitor-based group in both comparisons.
We concluded conversion to an mTOR inhibitor-based regimen
probably does not confer any benefit on BKVAN.
Schneidewind 2020 (267 participants) was a systematic review
looking at leflunomide in the treatment of BKVAN in kidney
transplant patients. There was no correlation between leflunomide
serum levels and virus reduction, but there were increased adverse
events. We found that although the leflunomide derivative FK778
decreased BK viral load, it was associated with a less favourable
rejection profile and kidney function and a higher incidence
of serious adverse events compared with immunosuppression
reduction.
A U T H O R S '   C O N C L U S I O N S
Implications for practice
High certainty evidence suggests that intensive screening is
efective in improving BK virus infection outcomes as it helps with
early detection of the infection and allows for a timely reduction
in immunosuppression reduction. Immunosuppression reduction
is the cornerstone for the management of BK virus infection.
Fluoroquinolones may not improve BK virus outcomes but may
slightly reduce the risk of graf loss. This efect is potentially related
to lower rates of UTIs and the development of de novo DSAs, but
more studies are required to make any concrete inferences. Their
use appears to be associated with better graf function. Once again,
this efect could be explained by lower rates of UTIs, but more
studies are needed. Of the CNIs, TAC probably has lower rates of
rejection, while CSA probably decreases BK viraemia and results
in less NODAT. There is no diference in the risk of BK viraemia
between MMF and AZA, but the risk of death and malignancy is
probably reduced with MMF. Conversion of either MMF or TAC to an
mTOR inhibitor may make little or no diference to graf loss, BK
viraemia, BK viruria and BKVAN. Leflunomide derivative FK778 may
have little or no efect on graf loss and BKVAN but may decrease
kidney function and increase aggravated hypertension.
Implications for research
This is the first systematic review that has looked at all RCTs for
BKVAN interventions. There is perhaps some evidence for lower BK
viraemia with CSA and this needs to be explored further in larger
studies reporting on similar outcomes.
We were unable to give clarity on the use of IVIG and cidofovir
as no RCTs were identified. RCTs of these interventions in kidney
transplant recipients, looking at BK viraemia, viruria, BKVAN, and
graf health, will add to the much-needed data.

Study characteristics
Methods
Study design
•
Open-label, parallel RCT
•
Study duration: 27 December 2000 to 29 October 2002
•
Duration of follow-up: 5 years
•
Setting: single centre
•
Country: USA
Participants
Study characteristics
•
Inclusion criteria: all patients aged >18 years, kidney transplant recipients
•
Exclusion criteria: previous treatment with rabbit anti-T cell polyclonal agents or allergy to rabbit pro-
teins; malignancy (except skin cancers in previous 2 years); serologic evidence of infection with HIV-1,
HTLV-1 or Hep B; use of an investigational agent in prior 4 weeks; inability to comply with protocol in
the opinion of the investigators; pregnant or nursing females
Baseline characteristics
•
Number: intervention group 1 (134); intervention group 2 (66)
•
Mean age ± SD (years): intervention group 1 (44 ± 13); intervention group 2 (46 ± 13)
•
Sex (M): intervention group 1 (86); intervention group 2 (40)
Interventions
Intervention group 1
•
FK506: initiated at 0.1mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses aiming trough levels 5 to 10 ng/mL
Intervention group 2
•
CSA: started at 8 mg/kg in 2 divided doses 12-hour trough level target 250 to 300 ng/mL during first 3
months and 100 to 250 ng/mL subsequently
Co-interventions
•
All patients except 6 antigen-matched living-related allograft recipients were induced with ATG
•
Adjuvant agents
◦ AZA: 5 mg/kg/day for 3 days then 2.5 mg/kg/day (dose then adjusted per WBC count) (under certain
circumstances AZA not used e.g. history of gout, PRA > 20%, second transplant, GN)
◦ MMF: 1000 mg twice/day
◦ Pred: 1 mg/kg/day, tapered by third month to 5 to 7.5 mg daily

Notes
Additional information
•
Originally a 1-year prospective trial. This is the retrospective 5-year review of this trial
•
Plasma and urine samples for BK-virus PCR were collected pre-transplant, weekly for 16 weeks, and
at months 5, 6, 9 and 12
•
Identification of BK viraemia triggered discontinuation of AZA or MMF. If viraemia failed to clear in 3
to 4 weeks, the CNI dose was reduced (CyA trough target 100 to 200, FK506 trough target 3 to 5)
•
All patients who developed an unexplained elevation of SCr underwent a kidney biopsy

Open-label, parallel RCT

Participants
Study characteristics
•
Inclusion criteria: 18 to 70 years; first or second kidney transplant recipients; cadaveric or living donors
•
Exclusion criteria: multi-organ or dual kidney transplants; PRA > 50%; non-heart bearing donor; HCV
or HBV positive donor; HIV; cold ischaemia time > 24 hours; malignancy or history of malignancy
Baseline characteristics
•
Number (randomised/analysed): 690/682; intervention group 1 (336); intervention group 2 (346)
•
Mean age ± SD (years): intervention group 1 (47.0 ± 11.9); intervention group 2 (46.3 ± 13.6)
•
Sex (M): intervention group 1 (241); intervention group 2 (225)
Interventions
Intervention group 1
•
CSA-ME: initiated within 24 hours of transplantation at 10 mg/kg/day, adjusted to achieve a C2 target
of 1600 ng/mL (range 1400 to 1800 ng/mL) during month 1, 1400 ng/mL (range 1200 to 1600 ng/mL)
during months 2 to 3 and 1000 ng/mL (range 800 to 1200 ng/mL) during months 4 to 6
Intervention group 2
•
TAC: initiated at a dose of 0.2 mg/kg/day within 24 hours post-transplant, adjusted to achieve C0 with-
in the range of 10 to 15 ng/mL during months 1 to 3 and 5 to 10 ng/mL during months 4 to 6
Co-interventions
•
All patients received MMF, or EC-MPS, administered according to local practice but initiated within
24 hours of graf reperfusion. Different MMF or EC-MPS dosages were permitted in the two treatment

Methods
Study design
•
Parallel, placebo-controlled RCT
•
Duration of follow-up: 12 months
•
Setting: single centre
•
Country: USA
Participants
Study characteristics
•
Inclusion criteria: kidney transplant recipients ≥ 18 years; 1 to 10 years post kidney transplanta-
tion from a deceased or living donor; stable kidney allograft function (within 20% baseline eGFR)
and based on the clinical judgement of the investigator; preserved kidney allograft function de-
fined as an eGFR ≥ 25 mL/min/1.73 m; UACR ≥ 30 ug/mg; ability of the participant, or their legally
authorised representative, to provide informed consent; women of non-childbearing potential do
not need to undergo pregnancy testing or agree to use adequate contraception; Women of child-
bearing potential can only be included if a pregnancy test is negative at the screening visit and if
they agree to use adequate contraception during the study and until 8 weeks after the last study
intervention dose
•
Exclusion criteria: documented recurrent lupus nephritis, ANCA vasculitis, membranoprolifera-
tive glomerulonephritis (including C3 glomerulopathy); history of solid organ transplantation oth-
er than kidney; AKI requiring dialysis within 6 months prior to screening; uncontrolled hyperten-
sion with a sitting SBP ≥ 180 mm Hg or DBP ≥ 100 mm Hg; any indication for treatment with a
steroidal MRA; UACR > 3500 mg/g at screening; CV event within 3 months prior to screening; elec-
tive percutaneous coronary intervention within 1 month prior to screening; known hypersensi-

Item is assessing the representativeness of exposed individuals in the community, not the representativeness of the sample of women
